summary:
Farmers often lose a season and are left guessing why. Was it really too dry? Too hot? Or was it something else? The weather record that could answer this already exists, but it rarely reaches the people who need it.

Season Check changes that. It opens NASA POWER's free daily weather record for any farm, going back to 1981, and places one season next to every normal year. Instead of charts and numbers, the farmer sees one clear sentence and a simple Dry / Normal / Wet bar.

It's built for real farmers in places like South Punjab. It opens in Urdu, reads the answer out loud, and understands spoken Urdu, Punjabi and Saraiki. The farm's location comes from the phone or a tap on the map.

It doesn't give advice. It shows what the sky did and lets the farmer decide, then asks whether that matches what they saw in their own field.

We're open about the limits: the data covers roughly 50 km, and it can't see irrigation.
details:
Kisan Season Check

What it does

Season Check helps a farmer answer one question: Was that bad season really unusual, or not?

The farmer selects a crop (rice or wheat), a year, and what they want to check: soil moisture, rainfall, or heat. The app retrieves NASA POWER's daily weather records for their exact location, going back to 1981. It then compares the selected season against every other season in the historical record.

The result is presented in plain language, such as "The soil was wetter than usual," alongside an emoji and a simple Dry / Normal / Wet bar showing where that year stands.

For those who want more information, a "More Details" section provides a day-by-day chart and all six measurements: daytime and nighttime temperature, humidity, rainfall, and topsoil and root-zone wetness.

How it works

Behind the scenes, the app retrieves daily data from the NASA POWER API and uses Python and pandas to rank the selected season against approximately 45 years of historical data.

Rainfall is ranked by its seasonal total, while the other measurements are ranked by their seasonal averages. The lowest 20% and highest 20% of historical years are classified as unusual, while the middle 60% are considered normal.

Built for real farmers

We designed Season Check for farmers who may not read English or may have limited literacy.

  • Urdu-first interface: The app opens in Urdu with right-to-left support, with English available in one tap.
  • Audio assistance: A Listen button reads the results aloud.
  • Multilingual voice input: Farmers can ask questions in Urdu, Punjabi, Saraiki, or English. For example, "chawal 2023 barish," and the app identifies the crop, year, and topic.
  • Easy location selection: Farmers can use their phone's GPS while standing in the field or select their location by tapping on an OpenStreetMap.

Benefits and impact

Farmers often explain a bad season based on memory and guesswork. Season Check gives them a quick, evidence-based way to compare their experience against 45 years of historical weather data.

The results might confirm what they already suspected or point towards other possible causes, such as disease, seed quality, or irrigation.

Importantly, Season Check does not tell farmers what to plant. It shows them what the weather did and leaves the decisions to them.

After every result, the app asks: "Does this match what you saw in your field?"

Over time, these responses can help identify where local farming experience and historical climate data agree, and where they differ.

Tools we used

  • Data: NASA POWER Daily Point API (Agroclimatology community)
  • Programming and analysis: Python, pandas, and Plotly for data processing and visualizations.
  • App and hosting: Streamlit, deployed through Streamlit Community Cloud using a public GitHub repository.
  • Voice input: OpenAI Whisper (large-v3), accessed through Groq's free API for speech-to-text.
  • Audio output: Browser's built-in text-to-speech functionality.
  • Maps and location: OpenStreetMap, Folium, and browser geolocation.
  • Database: Supabase, used to store farmers' feedback.
  • Hardware: Any phone or laptop with a web browser.

The application uses free-tier services, making it free to access and operate within the available service limits.

What makes it creative

Most climate tools are designed for scientists and present information through complex charts and technical measurements.

Season Check takes 45 years of NASA data and turns it into one simple sentence that a farmer can understand and hear in their own language.

But what makes it different is that we don't want to replace farmers' knowledge with technology. Instead of simply giving advice, the app asks farmers for their perspective.

We believe local knowledge is something worth recording, understanding, and learning from, not replacing.

What we considered

1. Honesty and data limitations

NASA POWER provides estimates representing an area of roughly 50 km, rather than measurements from an individual field. Its soil moisture estimates are also based on rainfall and do not capture canal irrigation. We clearly communicate these limitations to users within the app.

2. Data quality

We noticed that NASA's newest near-real-time values can sometimes change abruptly when the underlying data source switches. For example, at Multan, soil wetness suddenly dropped from 0.40 to 0.30 on 1 October 2026.

To avoid presenting potentially misleading information as a drought signal, the app excludes the latest three months of data.

3. Privacy

We do not store farmers' names or voice recordings. Location data is rounded to approximately 1 km to protect users' privacy.

4. Reliability

NASA data is cached to reduce repeated API requests and help the application remain usable on weak internet connections.

5. Language accessibility

The Urdu interface was drafted with AI assistance. We acknowledge that it still needs review and validation by a native Urdu speaker.

6. Scope and limitations

Season Check was initially developed around one farm and one farmer. It is a first test of the concept, not proof that the results will generalize across all of Punjab.
